utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I understand you have some matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to be very brief. Two days ago we discussed a translation, and we were supposed to put forward our position the next day. If we cannot do that today in the absence of Mr. Whiting, I would link this to another issue that the Chamber has raised yesterday, and if you allow me to give you a short explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will be about the other issue because I think it would be preferable to have the submissions made when Mr. Whiting is here, unless, Mr. Waespi, are you in a position to -- to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes I will be, Mr. President, but only after the next break, because I do have a small file on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear the submissions on the translation matter immediately after the next break. So I'll hear you on the other matter which you have to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand and appreciate that. But yesterday in the middle of my examination I found myself in a situation where I was compelled to answer a very delicate question. It is related to this document, and it referred to a medical record and you asked me where my questioning was leading. At that moment I said what I said, and I stand by that, but in order to avoid any further misunderstandings -- and I'm not sure whether I will be capable of doing that -- let me say a few things. I really largely shortened my cross-examination not to address any other issues that I intend to raise in my Defence case together with my team. The crux of the matter is that what the Prosecutor is duty bound to do is to prove beyond a reasonable doubt what is being alleged in the indictment. As Defence counsel, it is my duty to point to all the facts that increase this doubt up to the point that I can deny the whole incident. I'm going to pursue this line further on, and I will keep insisting on establishing the facts. I don't like to use proverbs or Latin phrases, but let me say something in my language that I recently wrote about, and that is, give me the facts, I will give you the law, and I can amend that by saying this, and that is, give me the facts, I will give you the law, and that eventually leads to justice. I will do my best all the time to deal and establish only the facts in order to assist you and the Defence of the accused. I will never put the victims in a situation where they will feel belittled or to deny that they had suffered. Even if they haven't -- when they didn't suffer, it is my duty to dispute that, and I felt it was my duty to try to explain to -- this to you; however, whenever you feel that you need to intervene, I will abide by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Can we have the witness in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, may I invite you to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, let us continue where we left off yesterday, and I will ask you again if you are able, of course, I'm not going to stop you, but I would prefer as short answers as possible.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the questions raised on the basis of what the Prosecutor asked to you explain was that the shop that you owned before the conflict handed over to the BH army for use. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. My shop where I worked, I only repaired vehicles, mostly golf cars, if a policeman had an accident or a glass was broken, I replaced and that was the whole cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then I will go back to your statement -- I'm not going to do it now, but I'm going to point this out to you once we come to your statement. Can you tell me, as a member of the reserve forces of MUP Sarajevo, who was in command of your units, police units? Can you tell me his name?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know. I had my station chief. I knew him, but I didn't know anyone else. I had no contact with him, I was just an ordinary policeman. I had no business dealing with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that not in a single action related to military affairs as a reserve police, you not take part?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You did not have an ordinary rifle; you had a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a semi-automatic rifle. I cannot even assemble or disassemble it even if you gave me 100.000 German marks this very minute. But I did carry one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This semi-automatic rifle you never used; that's what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there another policeman nearby across the street, armed just like you were with a machine-gun and a pistol?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever was in the police was issued with weapons. Whether they took -- took it with them home or left it at the station I don't know. There was not enough rifles, so we had to give rifles to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not what I asked you. I asked you whether -- in close proximity where you were, was another policeman on duty or on guard? Or I don't know how to qualify it.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two of us. I was there and another colleague of mine. We were securing the municipal building of Novi Grad municipality. There were two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On that day and the preceding days and the days afterwards, were there any conflict between the two parties?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to the front line. All I know was that there was shooting on a daily basis. There was not a single day that Sarajevo was not being shelled all over the place. I am not a detective or an inspector to keep track of that. I myself saw this one particular shell where it came and then I saw another one. It hit my house and I saw the direction, but as for the others, I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not what I asked you. I didn't ask but the shelling of Sarajevo. I believe you, what you are say being that. But my question was whether any shells were fired from Sarajevo at the opponents' position?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea whether there were any such weapons in Sarajevo at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you think that on the 26th of May, 1996, were loud explosions by NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear when Lukavica was being bombed, I was at my workplace. But I don't know who was bombing what and what was actually happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Safeta Hadzica Street where the incident that you described yesterday when the Prosecutor examined you happened, how far is this street from Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Mojmilo hill is about 150 metres from my house. That is where the hill begins, 150 metres. This is just roughly speaking. I didn't measure the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the ridge of Mojmilo hill, is it approximately 3 kilometres long?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Mojmilo hill, well, I really can't tell you. Whatever I say, I'll probably be wrong, believe me. I suppose that Mojmilo hill should be between 6 and 7 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking to you be accurate. You said what you said. Was the BH army occupied by BH army -- was this hill occupied by BH army?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. I never went to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, would it be fair to say that Mojmilo hill obstructs the view of both Lukavica and Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. I could see Ilidza, but I couldn't see Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since Hrasno hill is also nearby, how far it is from your house?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hrasno Brdo, well, could be 3 or 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you know who held this hill, which army?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know who was on the Zuc hill, either?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I were a commander, I would possibly be able to answer this question. I am just an ordinary policeman. I just observed things. That was all. I was just watching shells falling, and I don't know who was fighting who, who was attacking whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday you said that you saw the flight of the shell approaching your neighbourhood; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you also said that it flew at a low speed, that you could see it very well, and that it hit the roof of the building that you showed us?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what happened after it hit the roof?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was watching it. It was coming slowly from up there, and I thought it was an aeroplane and I thought it was a jet aeroplane descending and I thought to myself, it's flying so low, it's going to hit the building. No sooner had I thought that than it hit the building and there was a strong detonation and explosion and I was afraid that my wife and children, my brothers --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You explained that yesterday. I'm asking you to tell me after it had hit the roof, what happened with it? I'm not going to lead you, but I may just suggest to you, did it continue flying or did it remain on the roof?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It penetrated the roof one slab and then the next slab. It blew the windows and doors out. It was a very powerful detonation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. I never doubted that for a moment, but can you please just tell me. You said something yesterday, and I see that you know very little about those things. You said yesterday it was fired from a launching pad. Can you please explain how you know something like that and what is a launching pad, can you explain that for our benefit?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I served my term in the JNA and I saw that sort of thing being used in the army. That's why I know that you need a launching pad, a motor-propelled launching pad to launch a shell like this. And the range is not particularly big.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Not necessarily. They can be dropped from planes, can't they? But how did you know they were using launching pads to fire these shells?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one was. I have a preference for telling the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But when the war began, sir, it wasn't just the people on the other side who had JNA weapons. It also the BH army that had got hold of considerable amounts of weapons that had formally belonged to the JNA. Was that not the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one thing I know, and that is the truth. The JNA had the whole array of truly powerful weapons. Each of us had to pay into the communal kitty to get those weapons. All I know is that eventually, the only ones who got to use the weapons were the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say the Serbs. But who was it who was living on the other side of Mojmilo, people who used to be your neighbours until the very day the war began? Who was there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both Serbs and Muslims, but they were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Those who used to live there before the war, right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would have to show you a document now. This is from the 65 ter list, 00139A. This is an official report dated the 1st of June, 1995. It's about the incident on the 26th of May, 1995, the incident addressed by this witness. Let's start with the last page. There's a translation of this document. Can the witness look at page 1, first, please. We don't have the English yet, do we? Can we have the English on our screens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you're going to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. There is an ERN number of the English version. This is 00846948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you see the report, don't you? It's an official report.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can't see a thing. You could pay me, I still couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll try to zoom in. Can you see anything now?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through a glass darkly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here, you can have my glasses.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I use special glasses. I'm 60 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm 70 years old. My eyesight is still okay.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I need my special glasses for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, you recall me present and then the Defence counsel -- that yesterday the witness indicated that he had forgotten his glasses at home. Perhaps, if the relevant parts could be read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I find that acceptable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is no problem at all. As far as I'm concerned, I'll be glad to oblige.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, it says here, Ministry of the Interior, Sarajevo, the 1st of June, 1995, official report, in relation to the 26th of May, 1995, which is the day when the bomb fell. Can you accept for a fact that this is what the report is about, just based on my reading, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I accept that this report for a fact, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Can you accept, that since I read to you what the report said, this is true?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it must be true if my police station was the one who produced the report then it must be true, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please go to the last page in both English and B/C/S, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And let me read another portion of the document to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There, we have it now, but we have no English. Look at the last paragraph, please. I'll tell what you it says. "In addition to the injured, the following persons witnessed the shelling," and then there is a list of names of which I won't be reading to you, but one of the names on the list is your name, Dzemaludin Luinovic from Sarajevo, permanently residing at, and then your street address is stated. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I was wounded and injured?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that you were an eye-witness to the incident?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you one thing. When I realised that the shell had impacted inside, I didn't go there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not what I'm asking you, Witness, is it? Can you please confirm what it says here, that they interviewed you and that you were one of the eye-witnesses. That's what I'm putting to you. That's what I'm reading out to you. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am an eye-witness to the impact of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Further up the page it says a modified air bomb fell on the roof of a residential building, wounding several persons in the process and causing a considerable amount of material damage to the nearby buildings. That's what the report says. If that's what the report says, can you accept that as something that is recorded there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now go back to page 1. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 1, first you see the names, the people who were in charge of the investigation, and then two paragraphs down, you see paragraph 3. It says that what you saw fell, it hit the roof, it exploded, and -- no, no. This is what it says: "One explosive device, a powerful one, and that on this occasion, several persons were injured." That's one part of the sentence. So I might as well go on and read the whole thing, but I don't wish to tire the Chamber with this. They will soon realise why I'm doing this. You spoke about the fact that this was a very powerful shell and that it caused injuries to several persons in the building on top of which the shell landed. If that's what it says, can you confirm that for a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing. I did realise -- I did see that people had been injured, but I did not take any details from those people. It was the police inspectors who took their personal details because that was their job, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I would like to go on and read the next line back to you, the following paragraph. It says: "An on-site investigation was conducted on the scene itself and it's immediate surroundings. It was established that, in the vicinity of the residential building at Safeta Hadzica Street and then the number is stated, several artillery missiles had landed, causing no injury to any person." That's what it says, sir. Can we take that at face value, what they recorded here?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with this statement. No injuries were caused to anyone by those small shells that followed the big shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to your statements, sir. These have been admitted as OTP exhibits. The first one is P00297; I want page 2 of that statement, please. My apologies, P00298; that's the first thing we have to tackle. Page 2, I'll start with paragraph 7. Here, sir, you say: "I can remember clearly the day that our neighbourhood was shelled. It was on the 26th of May. It must have been around 11.00 a.m. I have had been mobilised in to the reserve force of the police, so I was on duty on that day." Is that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the statement goes on to say: "I suddenly heard a loud noise like a plane about to land, and I saw something flying in from the direction of Ilidza. Soon after I heard a powerful explosion." Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Paragraph 8. "Although I was on duty and was not supposed to leave my post, I ran across to my flat because I feared for the lives of my family, my father and daughter were standing outside." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So despite the fact that this bomb had landed, you found your father and your daughter out in the street; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't out in the street. They were in the front yard in front of my house. They were crying. My old man was really angry, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: They were outside the house any way, outside the flat; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the distance might have been perhaps 25 to 30 metres between my house and my father's house, so they just walked out into the front yard to see what exactly was going on. My daughter was crying. My father started crying, too. I told them to go to our neighbour's house and take cover in the basement, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But nobody had been injured up to this point; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the first big shell fell, there was some people who were injured inside the building. But I didn't go there, I just went to my own home to make sure that none of family had were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what you say here. Okay. We can take that at face value if you like. You told them to go back inside; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So I went back inside and I took cover. Because, based on previous experience, I knew --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said yesterday --

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- that there would be other shells following; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I suspect, in fact, I know the interpreter is having a hard time keeping up with you. You're going too fast and not observing the pause between question and answer. That applies to the witness and to Mr. Tapuskovic. Do you understand that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're entirely right, Your Honour. I'm trying to keep track of time and then I forget all about this. If I have been looking at my screen -- well, okay, I'll start looking at my screen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on your experience, you knew that there would be more shells coming; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was just a thing that normally happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say -- you go on to say, "my predictions eventually proved true"; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Several minutes later, the same building that had been hit was showered with other smaller shells; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't that the building was hit, it was around the building and in the direction of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm reading to you is your own statement to OTP investigators back in 2006 on the 26th of April. You said, literally, "that same building that had been hit was showered with other smaller shells." Are you trying to challenge that statement? Are you telling us that that is not true?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm telling you is that no other shell fell on that building; other shells did fall around it. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But look how it goes on, this is what you say: "The shells partially damaged my home too. Fortunately, no one in my family was injured." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now, please, sir, can you focus on the following words, especially because this is part of your statement, this paragraph 9 of your statement. Pay close attention, please. "After the shelling had stopped and I came out of the house, I learned that during the shelling many people had been injured. It was only after the shells had landed," as you say here, that you learned that many persons, many people had been wounded. Is that what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that no one was injured around my home. I don't know about further afield. I couldn't possibly go moving about under all these shells that were falling down on us. I had to look after myself. Somebody probably was killed, but I am no super man. I can't keep running around just to check who was killed when or why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But this is what I'm putting to you the difference is. You say that after the first shell there were no injured or casualties in general. You say here that the casualties were caused by the shells that followed, that landed on the area. I'll tell you something else. Are you denying there what you said in that first statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm telling you, which -- or in certain knowledge, a shell that big landing on top of a building causing no casualties, that would be the first, but I leave it to you to interpret that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not construing anything. I'm just dealing with your statement and what you claim to have seen and what was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have witness's statement P00298, given on the 26th of April, 2006. No, I don't know what I'm doing any longer. It's actually P00297, dated 10th of March, 1997. And if we could move now to page 2, please. Let me go back for a minute to the issue of your workshop. You answered these questions and corrected it during the examination-in-chief. However, I have to return to this topic. Look at paragraph 3, which reads that "on the 15th of May, 1992, I was appointed a reserve policeman which I continued until 8th of January, 1996" which means that after the war finished, you remained a member of the reserve forces until January 1996.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until demobilisation and everybody knows when that took place. That is when the whole reserve force was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you just said --

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. And then you went on to say, during the war, my private workshop was also used as a workshop of the BH army. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how big your workshop was where you repaired cars?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you ever came to Sarajevo, you know how they look like. They were not big ones. Here in Holland they have rather sizeable workshops. So it was about seven by three metres. And if you believe I was capable of doing anything major there -- and it was specifically intended for car repairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting to you that at that time this workshop was used in order to camouflage certain things; for example, mortars?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me draw your attention now to the penultimate passage which says: "I went to the scene of the shelling." Can you see it? Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say here: "I went to the scene of the shelling and assisted my colleagues, meaning the policemen; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no policemen there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What kind of colleagues are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were people. I don't know whether it was UNHCR, whether it was UNPROFOR. People heard a detonation, an explosion. They came around, collected and picked up the injured, took them to the hospital. I don't know a single person by name. Sometimes you live with some people next door to them and you don't -- never learn their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you say here that several journalists also came to the spot.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some came and took pictures. There were inspectors there, compiling records and they found a piece of this bomb that hit my house. They took it away with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But look at the last sentence. "In fact, within ten minutes of the first blast referred to above, six other shells fell within an area of about 100 square metres."

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by this. After this big shell, none of those shells hit the same building, but they rather went towards the police station. There were five or six of them. Now, whether anyone was killed there, to tell you the truth, I didn't dare venture out of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a number of documents that I would like to present to the witness, and with that I would conclude my cross-examination. Firstly, Your Honours, although we requested several translations, we haven't received a single one to date. Actually, a few. But in any case, of the hundreds and hundreds of documents that we have, we have not been given translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let mow now show you a document signed by Fikret Prevljak, the brigade commander concerning the incident of the 26th of May, 1995. There's an important fact with is related to the evidence given by this witness. This is DD00-0953. That's the BH republic document. And since the witness doesn't have glasses, I think I should read it out to him. Let me read this report to you. First, they talk about the aggressor, and let me read it to you, what this commander, Fikret Prevljak, reported about what he observed in the behaviour of the aggressor, and he says as follows: "At 1838 they fired a modified aerial bomb at Svrakino Selo from Butmir." Can you tell me where that is?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to any military reports, I can't give you any answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But he doesn't mention at all in this report that anything came to the area that you were in.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my report. I cannot comment on military reports. I made my own report and there's the record of what happened. I can only talk about what I see as truth and about my record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could it be that Svrakino Brdo was the place where you were?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You had a chance to see the photograph. There was no hill there. It was one of the most beautiful locations in Sarajevo and I couldn't have wished for a better place to live in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Everybody in the former Yugoslavia loved Sarajevo. Now, let us look at what he says about "our forces" and he means your forces. It reads: Our forces did not respond to artillery fire in the last 24 hours, while members of the 115th Mountain Brigade returned fire only on two occasions. Therefore, it shows that there was fire coming from Sarajevo, although you claim otherwise. This was the report dated the 26th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, let me tell you one thing. This is a military report and what we saw before was a MUP report. I stand by the MUP report and my report because they contain the truth. As far as this military report is concerned, I cannot -- or, rather, I have no right to stand by it and corroborate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly the point how it is possible that there is discrepancy between a report compiled by the BH army and the MUP? Can you explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think the witness has been clear. He was stationed as a reserve policeman in this area, a part of Sarajevo, and how can he possibly comment on what appears to be a brigade commander reporting to the first command of -- to the command of the 1st Corps of the ABiH reports about any ABiH response somewhere in Sarajevo? I think that's an answer the witness cannot give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, it's not his discrepancy. Proceed to another matter, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The essence of my question was this document. I'm not insisting, but time will come for it to be tendered. I didn't insist on it so much and on this particular aerial bomb but rather on the fact that there was fire coming from Sarajevo, and that what is this report claims. I would like the witness to tell me:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any shooting going out of Sarajevo? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, witness, you're being asked to repeat your answer for the benefit of the interpreter, and ours as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I need to hear the question first again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the document that I just read out to you, it shows that BH army units were responding, as they say, to the fire coming from the Serbian side. Did you hear any fire from Sarajevo? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think the question itself is fine: Did you hear any fire, you know, based on his knowledge and based on what we know where he was standing. If it's confined to that issue, that's fine. But putting, you know, comments from these documents to this witness and asking him whether that's correct or not, that's why I objected a minute ago, and I thought Your Honours ruled on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the question is: Did you hear any fire from Sarajevo? Witness, what's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer to that is, honestly speaking, I wasn't on the front line. They were further away from me and I have no idea, frankly speaking. The only thing I could hear was shelling landing in our neighbourhoods. Otherwise, I didn't hear anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since he said that he didn't hear anything, then I am not allowed, I presume, to offer this for identification, and I would like to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, we don't have an objection to it being identified -- marked for identification. But before it's tendered, we just need to have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will be marked for identification as Exhibit D94.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a document here with me. It's an UNPROFOR report of 26 May 1995, and with your leave, I would like to show it to the witness. It refers to Sector Sarajevo, and I would like to hear if he is able to comment on that. That's number DD00-0949. There's no translation of this document into English, but I translated this passage. Sector Sarajevo, page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Just to make the record clear, the original of this document is in English, and I understand that there is no translation into B/C/S. Just following on the previous document, we will do a draft translation with our resources, so the Defence doesn't need to wait until -- or initiate a double translation, so you're aware of it. And once it's finished, we can forward it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me read out to the witness only this portion referring to Sector Sarajevo. "Item 2: The situation was tense with an increased level of firing. Detonations were reported in the traditional hot spots." And there's mention of a second air-strike. My question is: Did he hear these detonations in his neighbourhood as well as the detonations that took place on the opposite side as a result of fire from the weapons belonging to the BH army? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It seems that you are treating me as if I had been a general in the army. I was just an ordinary policeman. Your question is a matter for UNPROFOR and they are authorised to give you any reasonable explanation. If they compiled this report, it's not my place to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about this DD00-0949, the UNPROFOR report, 26th of May? Can that be admitted as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this the one that he says he knows nothing about? No, we can't admit that, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know. He says he doesn't know. He says this. If it's an UNPROFOR report, he doesn't doubt it. That's what he said. And this is an UNPROFOR report which says that there was intense firing on that day, an increase in firing. And that seems quite important in itself. He's not saying he doesn't know. He doesn't know about this report, but the report says that there was an increase in firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's really a lawyer's point. He says here that your question is a matter for, I presume, UNPROFOR, and they're authorised to give you any reasonable explanation. "If they compiled this report, it's not my place to comment on it." I think he's saying he doesn't know anything about it. In his own words, he says he's not a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did he hear that there was an increase in the firing on that day? That's what I'm wondering about and that's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, if I could clarify. I think the general rule that the Chamber is trying to establish is that there has to be some sort of relation between the witness and the document before you can enter the document through that witness. In this case, it seems that no relation can be established, so this is why the Chamber isn't willing to admit this document through this witness. You may seek to introduce it through another witness, but there is no relation in this case, so the answer is no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now understand fully, and I will do my best in the future to comply with this properly. I take your point. I would like to finish with another report. First, I'd like to ask the witness:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday something about this occurring on the spot, the first two shells not exploding. Is that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of the shells exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly yesterday when you said that one did not explode?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the shell that hit my house first impacted against the tarmac. It ricochetted and smashed into my house, drilling a hole 2 by 2 metres large. And there was a piece of the shell that was left right there on the ground. The inspectors arrived. They carried out an on-site investigation and they took this fragment away to be submitted for analysis by the police experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the other shell? Did that one explode?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which other one? There is only one that hit my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just ask you this: I showed you that report about the injured and the air bomb that fell the way you described; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Among the injured there were about eight persons who were well along, as you said. For example, Hatic Zaim.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know your own neighbour?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him. All the faces were familiar, but I couldn't put a name to each of the faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about Muharem Begovic? Was he a BH army member, for example?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, but I'd like to make a brief comment about that UN document that we just discussed, or Your Honours discussed with the Defence. I agree that there was no foundation laid with this witness to have it admitted, but in itself the document appears to be, you know, a UN document, and we usually rely on these types of documents. So if that goes in as kind of a self-propelled document which speaks for itself - it just says what it says - related to the day one of our incidents occurred, the 26th of May, 1995, we don't have an objection to come in through that kind of different procedural door than by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider that and make a decision later. Mr. Luinovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I could be excused very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. The next witness is Mr. Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Please state your full name; your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Enes Jasarevic; 29 November 1958; Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I lead the witness through his background?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, is it correct that before the war you were an electrician?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, following your ruling yesterday, may I please go into private session for this one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jasarevic, during the war, and in particular the period 1994 to 1995, did you work at a transformer station in Sarajevo as an electrician?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a maintenance technician for a high-voltage transmitter that distributed electricity throughout the whole of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in which district or where was that transformer station located?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It was near Novi Grad municipality, near the radio and television building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I was to show you a map, would you be able to mark the location on that map?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that 65 ter 02872 be shown on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you'll soon see a map on your screen -- no, no, it's just about to come up. Just a couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we zoom the map, please. In particular, sort of veering towards the left-hand side. Is it possible to zoom in one more part, one more bit? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, are you able now to see where your transformer station was?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The court usher is going to hand you a marker. And before you mark anything, just wait for my instructions. So please mark with a circle where the transformer station was that you worked in.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And to the side, on the right-hand side, can you put the letter T, please.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: On this map, do you also see the TV building, the Bosnian television building?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can you mark that with the letters TV, please.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Approximately how far was your transformer station from the TV building?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: About 100 metres perhaps just over 100 metres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to ask you a few questions about the transformer station. Just very, very briefly, what is it that the transformer -- what was done there at the transformer building -- station?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: You mean on that particular day or generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It's a transformer station. Employees worked there. That's where the high voltage came that was then transformed into low voltage and then distributed for the benefit of the population. We had our offices there. Whenever any action on our part was needed in any part of town, we would just go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that the low voltage was distributed for the benefit of the population. In which particular areas was this low voltage distributed; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, Novi Grad. Some of it went to Dobrinja --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this transformer station we mostly distributed to Novi Grad, Alipasino Polje, Dobrinja, and other parts of town. I'm not sure how far. You couldn't distribute throughout the city from this one transformer station. It only covered one part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were there other -- well, in the period 1994/1995, were there other transformer stations functioning in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Should I name them?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, no, it's okay. What can you say about the distribution of -- let's say the frequency of electricity or energy distribution in the city throughout the period in 1994/1995? Was it constant, was it intermittent?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no regularity. It would be evenly distributed across Sarajevo. Some parts of Sarajevo were out of electricity and then they had electricity again and they -- they all took turns like that and that was all they had. Sometimes ducts were interrupted that crossed the confrontation lines and certain areas would suffer power cuts. We covered whatever we could. It's called power cuts, you know, sometimes you don't have electricity for five or six hours at a time, that sort of thing. We call it power cuts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And why were there power cuts or why were some parts of Sarajevo without electricity? Do you know the reasons for that search?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Because Sarajevo does not have its own source of energy. We got all of it through overhead lines, and once those broke down, there was nothing left to distribute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And these overhead lines, you say once those broke down -- how did they break down, or why did they break down? If you know.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: On account of the fighting. This normally occurred along the confrontation lines, the front lines. And then UNPROFOR would come and get us. We would do the job and mend what we could often under dangerous conditions since there was fighting going on, and sometimes we went out to parts of Sarajevo where there was no fighting in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Moving now to the transformer station, you said there were other colleagues that worked there. Who did you work with?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: With my colleagues, my fellow electricians, the same people who did the job before the war and throughout the war. But that was our job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you have a supervisor?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We had a supervisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It was the late Sulejman Prasko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of -- of any of your other colleagues?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Sure, I do. Specifically, Slato Salko, at least as far as this incident is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you've just said now "this incident." When you say "this incident," do you know firstly the date on which this incident took place? And I'll get to the incident in a moment.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: This occurred on the 24th of May, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: On that day, did you go to work at the transformer station?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What time did you get to work?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Sometime between 8.00 and 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I actually want the witness sometime in the examination to mark further points on this map. I just hope that the image is not going to be lost if I leave it on there. I would appreciate some guidance from the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The best way of proceeding would to be save this image and then we can add further markings on it after we assign an exhibit number to it, if ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can give it an exhibit number now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this map will become Exhibit P300.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you said you got to work between sometime at 8.00 and 9.00. Now, when you reached work, that is, when you reached the transformer station, did you notice or witness any fighting or military activity in the vicinity of the station?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: You mean when I came to work?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, once you arrived at the station.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: There was no fighting nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in the vicinity of your station, in the area where the station was, there were any military, in other words, Bosnian government military facilities present?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No military ones. There was the municipal hall in front of us, the TV building, there was the waterworks across the way, behind us there was the school building and some residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: On that day when you got to the transformer station between 8.00 and 9.00, did you see any military personnel, that is soldiers, in the vicinity of your station?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you arrived at work, was there somewhere that you were supposed to go that morning?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was supposed to be a mission with UNPROFOR. They were supposed to get us, pick us up with their APC and then we would go to wherever we were supposed to go on a given day. We were supposed to go somewhere or other, but they failed to show up and some of them from the PTT, which is where they were billeted, phoned us to say there would be no mission on that day so stayed there and there was nothing for to us do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I think you touched upon this earlier on in the examination, but when you were to go with UNPROFOR, what was it that you were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. It's a live witness. But I still intend to finish within the 35 or 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, sure. You said that you were supposed to go on a mission with UNPROFOR, and I believe you touched upon what you do with UNPROFOR earlier on in the examination. But what was it that you were supposed to do on that day with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: One of the power lines had broken down. The one that supplied electricity to Vucapato [phoen]. That one also ran across confrontation lines. So whenever there was a breakage like that, we couldn't go on our own. We couldn't cross the confrontation lines. We had to be escorted to places like those by UNPROFOR. But the mission was cancelled on account of the fighting, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may suggest, this would be an appropriate time in my examination for a break. I just note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll break now for 20 minutes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, we don't have much more time, so I'm going to try to be as rapid as possible. When you were -- you just said that UNPROFOR did not come and therefore you were waiting around, had nothing to do. During the morning, in other words, from the time of 9.00 till, let's say, 11.00 in the morning, did you hear anything in particular, anything significant, at that time?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime, 10.00 or 11.00 - I cannot tell you precisely - something flew over, but the sound was very unusual. We were frightened because we had never heard anything similar before. It hit, but I don't know exactly where. Some of us got frightened and went downstairs to other rooms where there were cables and which offered some kind of shelter. However, nothing happened after that and we continued our duty, normally, that is, we were sitting around in our workplace but we didn't hear anything after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said the sound was very unusual. Can you describe what the sound -- describe the sound, please.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, how shall I explain it? At first it sounded like an aeroplane, but it wasn't an aeroplane. It was unusual in that it was nothing that we had heard before, although we heard many things before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You also said that: "It hit, but I don't know exactly where." When I say "it hit," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: We heard an explosion, a detonation. It was a projectile, but at the time I didn't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You say you didn't know exactly where, but are you able to tell the Court roughly where the explosion took place?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Since we were indoors, I think it flew over our heads and went on, probably towards the TV building or behind it. I didn't know exactly. I just know that it flew over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you hear the explosion?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We heard a kind of dull impact. It wasn't close enough to hear it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: After that, you said that: "Nothing happened and we continued our duty and we were sitting around our workplace." Did anything significant occur after that period, on that day?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because our working hours was coming to a close, we had nothing to do, so we intended to leave and go home. Sometimes after 1.00 p.m. there was nothing for us to do. So we called our families on the phone, because for me to reach my home I had to go to Dobrinja. So I asked them in everything was quiet there for me to get home safely, because everyone had to be -- had to follow what was going on, whether there was any fighting, before they set off for home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. You said you spoke to your family on the phone in Dobrinja and you asked them if everything was quiet there. What did the family member tell you?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It was sometime around 1.00 p.m. They told me that it was quiet, and then I told her that I would soon be coming home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So at that time, around 1.00, what did you and your other two colleagues that you mentioned earlier, what did you do? Did you leave the transformer station?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: We started to go home. My colleague, Salko Slato, lived in Mojmilo, so we covered part of the route together, while my foreman was living in another part of the town. I went out, as did my foreman, in front of the entrance. Since the other colleague who was supposed to accompany me was not there, I stayed a while with my foreman. While I was waiting for my colleague, there was a piece of earth surface which was sowed with some vegetables and it was covered with a plastic sheet. So he was weeding this little plot. I was standing next to him, waiting for my other colleague to join me on our way home. When he came downstairs, we went through the exit, said our good-byes to Sulejman Prasko, the late Sulejman Prasko, who told us, "I'll leave soon, just as soon as I finish weeding the plot." When the two of us passed through the gate, and maybe we walked some 10 metres or so, we heard an impact, and the consequences of that impact are well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say you heard an impact, what kind of -- well, what kind of sound was that?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: My colleague and I passed the gate and we heard something which I said I believed was an aeroplane, and I said to him, "How come there are planes flying?" We looked up. We didn't see any aeroplane; however, the sound was coming closer and closer and becoming stronger and stronger. Suddenly, I think I saw a dark object which hit a pylon, which was inside the compound of the transformer station. There was a strong flash and I fell on the ground. Whether I fell there or I was pushed by the blast, I cannot tell you now. I fell on my stomach. While I was lying on the ground, the pylon that had been hit by the bomb started to collapse and I thought it was going to collapse on me. However, the power line stopped it from falling on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that you fell on your stomach after the flash. One second, sorry. Were you injured by this explosion?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If it's appropriate, would you be able to tell the Court what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: When I fell down, then the pylon collapsed. I turned over on my back and I noticed something on my right leg, and on my left leg as well. I saw a hole in my blue jeans, trouser leg, and there was a kind of contraction in my right arm. I tried to take off my jacket, my leather jacket; however, I couldn't do that because I couldn't detach it from my arm. A piece of shrapnel, which I later saw, hit me and attached the sleeve of the leather jacket to my elbow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you -- on account of your injury, did you have to go to the hospital after this incident?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what about your supervisor or, you said, foreman, Mr. Sulejman Prasko? What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Since he was on the inside of the fence and we were outside the fence, I took off my jacket and kept it on my elbow. The colleague of mine was slightly injured. We couldn't open the entrance gate, probably due to an impact, so he tried to jump over the fence in order to see what happened to the foreman. I also approached the fence and I saw Mr. Prasko lying there. He was moving his mouth, which means that he was still showing signs of life. Somebody came from the direction of the television; I think it was a woman a journalist. And then a blue -- a white car came along and people asked whether there were any casualties. They wanted to put us in this car and take us away, but we wanted to know what happened to him. "Are you going to take him?" The man said, "Let us first take care of you and somebody else will take care of him." They put us in the car and took us to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier on, when I asked you about your supervisor, you said "the late Sulejman Prasko." Do I take it from that answer that he eventually succumbed and died as a result of this incident?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. His lips were moving; that's what I saw. But somebody told me that he was already dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to show some photographs to the witness. Can 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: One minute, just one minute. [Interpretation] While we still have this map on the screen, could the witness show us where the first and the second shell or bomb came from? We know that the witness was in the transformer station. He said that the bomb arrived from the direction of Lukavica. Could he show this to us on the map, for the sake of clarity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is rather small. This is the place where we heard the sound. The sound was coming, I think at least, from Mojmilo hill, from that side. I may try to mark it on the map. Do you have any other map, because I really cannot ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Do we have another map?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I understand that we have. Perhaps it can be zoomed in a bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The court deputy is going to zoom in, but we will lose the mountains, he says, but -- the markings, the markings, but they've already been saved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is where I was standing, roughly speaking, I believe that this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, can I just obtain a clarification for the benefit of the Court. The direction that you have just drawn here, does that relate to the projectile that you were injured from and your supervisor was killed, or does it relate to the sound that you heard in the morning at around 10.00?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: This relates to this one, because in the morning, we were indoors and I couldn't specifically say which direction it came from. This is the second projectile, although this is not very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So "the second projectile," meaning the one that you were injured from?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm happy to have this map tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will become Exhibit P301, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May I now have the photographs brought up, and they are 65 ter 00079. Mr. President, pursuant to your ruling, I believe that I am over the 30 minutes assigned for my examination. I seek your leave to be another seven -- five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we will allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see some photographs on the screen there?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And are those photographs of the pylon that you spoke about earlier from your transformer station?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May we move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Similarly, are those photographs from your transformer station showing the pylon that had been knocked down by the projectile?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Witness, do these photographs depict your transformer station and the pylon?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I want to show the witness a picture of a deceased person and I would like to do this just for a second. I understand that it's not pleasurable viewing, but in light of the line the Defence have taken, I submit that, for evidentiary purposes, this would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you inform us, please, who took those photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: These photographs come from the investigation file and were taken by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may show it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since my colleague Sachdeva said what he said, I would like to hear from him to which particular part of our Defence case he was referring to. Since he told the Chamber that we have adopted a certain line of defence, I would like him to explain what he meant in order for to us take due care in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't consider that to be necessary. I'll ignore it and just consider that Mr. Sachdeva would like to show this photograph, and I have allowed him to show it. I attach no weight to the other part of the statement. We're ready to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May we move to -- I believe it's page 8 of this batch. If I could just give you the ERN number. It's 00375141. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the bottom photograph? Do you see a plan there?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Who is that man?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's the late Sulejman Prasko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The picture can be removed. And, Mr. President, I'd like to tender these photographs into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these pictures, photographs, will become Exhibit P302.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May I now have on the screen 65 ter number 03010.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, in a moment you will see another photograph, and I'm going to ask you one or two questions. Do you see a photograph there on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what is that a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the whole photograph, or do you want me to show you just the transformer station?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, yes, why don't you take the marker and put a T by the transformer station.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see the TV building in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can you mark that with the letters TV, please.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And where you've put the T for the transformer station, do you see the two pylons?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And are you able to mark the spot where the explosion took place and the pylon that was hit by the explosion? Just mark that with a cross, please.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the pylon that you are referring to, is that the one, if looking at the picture, on the left-hand side or the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I think it's on the left-hand side, closer to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P303, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Lastly, Witness, just a couple of final questions. You said to the Court that you lived in Dobrinja. During the period 1994/1995, was living in Dobrinja, was it -- was it a safe or a dangerous place?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It was very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And why was it dangerous?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, Dobrinja was surrounded on all sides. There was no communication with the town itself. There was a little communication, but it was quite dangerous to head for the centre. Could you have been hit from just about anywhere. It was a place where life was very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You say you could have been hit from just about anywhere. Was Dobrinja subjected to sniping and shelling during the period 1994/1995?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And just focussing on sniping, again during the period 1994 to 1995, was there a particular location or a place that was particularly dangerous or subjected, on a frequent basis, to sniping?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That place connected Dobrinja with the rest of the town. That was the only road, actually. You had to drive across and drive very fast. Whoever tried walking, this always proved a risky enterprise. There was non-stop firing. The road was under fire throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did the inhabitants assign a particular name or a phrase for that road that you talk about?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They called it the Road of Death; that's what they called it. It was quite dangerous. You had to drive across very fast. I even tried cycling across once, but it was a very risky thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you know where the sniping came from?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
